verses.translation_literal: A psalm, of Asaph. God, God, YHWH has spoken and has summoned [the] earth, from [the] rising of [the] sun to its setting.
verses.translation_dramatic: A psalm of Asaph. Hear it: the Strong One, God, the LORD, has spoken. His voice goes out and the whole earth is summoned, from the place where the sun first rises to the place where it goes down.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a courtroom opening, and the actor should play it as a herald's proclamation: three divine titles stacked one on another, each a heavier gavel-stroke. 'El' is the Strong One, 'Elohim' the supreme God and judge, and 'YHWH' the covenant name. KJV's 'mighty God, even the Lord' squeezes three words into two and hides the stacking, and its 'the Lord' is the usual substitution for the divine name; the Hebrew has the name itself. Ibn Ezra hears in the titles power to carry out judgment, eternity and unchanging presence. Radak reads 'Elohim' as 'judge of judges'.

The verb 'summoned' is the language of a court summons, not a casual call; the whole inhabited world is the audience, from sunrise to sunset, the ancient way of saying 'east to west', the full extent of the day. KJV's 'going down thereof' is fine in sense, but the Hebrew word מבוא is simply 'its entering', the sun going in to its home. The title 'of Asaph' (the preposition can mean by, for or belonging to the guild of Asaph, the temple singers) frames the psalm as sung liturgy; here a prophetic word is performed in the Temple.

philological_notes.note: Three divine names in a row, 'God, God, YHWH', as a solemn court announcement. Metzudat David takes 'El' as the one above all powers; Radak takes 'Elohim' as 'judge of judges'. The English versions split between 'God of gods' (YLT, BBE), 'the mighty God' (KJV, Webster) and 'the Mighty One, God' (ASV); the Hebrew has no 'of' between the names.
'And he summoned'. In judicial settings the verb means to call people to appear. Radak notes the past tense with a waw reads as a future event, a prophetic perfect for something certain.
'its entering', the sun's setting; Metzudat Zion cites 'for the sun had set' (Gen 28:11), where the same verb is used of the sun going in.

verses.translation_literal: From Zion, [the] perfection of beauty, God has shone forth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Out of Zion, that hill where beauty is gathered whole, God has blazed forth like dawn breaking over stone.
verses.directors_commentary:
The camera moves in from the whole earth to a single hill. Zion is named not for its height or its walls but as the 'perfection of beauty', a phrase the people use of the city in Lam 2:15, and the word for 'perfection' (mikhlal) carries the sense of everything gathered and complete (Metzudat Zion ties it to 'all', kol). The verb hofia' is the verb of light: God does not merely appear, he shines out, as a lamp or a dawn.

The KJV 'hath shined' is faithful but plain; the Hebrew choice of a light verb prepares the fire of the next verse. Mind the sound: the word for 'beauty' (yofi) and the verb for 'shone' (hofia') share the root-letters y-f, so the line is a quiet echo of itself. This is the god of one particular hill, in a world where every nation placed its god on a sacred mountain; the psalm claims that from this hill the whole earth is summoned.

philological_notes.note: 'Perfection of beauty': mikhlal is 'completeness', from kll 'to complete, include all'; the same noun-pattern is used of fine garments in Ezek 23:12 (cited by Metzudat Zion). Rashi explains it as a noun, glossing it with an Old French word.
Hiphil of yf', 'to shine forth'. Radak glosses it as equivalent to 'will shine' and ties it to the call to the nations; Metzudat Zion: 'lit up and shone'.

verses.translation_literal: Our God comes, and let him not be silent: fire before him devours, and around him it storms exceedingly.
verses.translation_dramatic: Our God is coming, and this time he will not hold his peace. Fire runs ahead of him, eating as it goes, and all about him the wind howls and tears at the air.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice shifts from narrator to the worshippers: 'our God'. Their wish and their warning are the same. The verb 'let him not be silent' is a negative wish, not a flat promise; Ibn Ezra says these are the words of the righteous who hope their enemies will be destroyed, and Rashi links it to Ps 79:10, the prayer for the shed blood of his servants. The KJV's 'shall come, and shall not keep silence' turns a prayer into a prediction, and it makes the fire future as well.

Silence here is the long delay of divine judgment; a God who 'keeps silence' is a God who lets wrong stand (see Ps 28:1, 83:2). Now he comes in the standard storm-god kit of the ancient Near East, fire ahead and tempest around, but this storm is not Baal's: the God of Israel is the one holding the lightning, and the people of the psalm have no other. The final word, 'exceedingly', is saved for the end of the verse; let the wind rise on it. Ibn Ezra notes that nis'arah is spelled with shin but means 'storm' (sa'ar).

philological_notes.note: Jussive of charash, 'to be silent'; with 'al it is a negative wish or prohibition rather than a statement of fact, so the line reads as a plea: 'let him not keep silent'.
Niphal of s'r 'to storm, be tempestuous'; Ibn Ezra says it is written with shin but is the same as sa'arah, 'storm wind'. Metzudat Zion: 'from the word for storm'.

verses.translation_literal: He summons to the heavens from above, and to the earth, to judge his people.
verses.translation_dramatic: From his height he calls to the heavens, and down to the earth he calls: come and witness, for he sits in judgment on his own people.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a courtroom, and the court is being assembled. In an ancient covenant lawsuit the judge calls on heaven and earth as witnesses, because they are the only parties that outlast every human oath (compare Deut 32:1; Isa 1:2). Notice who is on trial: not the foreign nations but 'his people'. The KJV reads 'that he may judge his people', which is accurate, but 'he shall call' loses the sense that the summons is going out right now.

The commentators split on who 'heaven' and 'earth' are. Ibn Ezra: the angels and the inhabitants of earth; Rashi: the heavenly prince of the nations and the kings of Egypt (Isa 24:21); Radak and Meiri: angels sent to take vengeance on the enemies, as at Sennacherib's camp. Play the line as a call to witnesses first; the reading about enemies is a later reading imposed on a psalm whose accused is Israel itself (v. 7).

philological_notes.note: 'To judge his people'. Rashi reads 'din' here as 'to avenge', as in Deut 32:36, 'for the LORD will judge his people'; the psalm itself, though, turns the judgment on Israel (v. 7).

verses.translation_literal: Gather to me my faithful ones, cutters of my covenant over sacrifice.
verses.translation_dramatic: Gather them to me, my faithful ones, the ones who sealed my covenant over the blood of the sacrifice.
verses.directors_commentary:
The judge speaks for the first time, and what he says first is a roll call. 'Faithful ones' (chasidai) are people bound by chesed, loyalty: the covenant partners. The Hebrew idiom is 'cutters of my covenant', because in the ancient Near East one 'cut' a covenant: the animal was split and the parties passed between the pieces (Gen 15), or its blood was sprinkled, as at Sinai in Exod 24:8, which Rashi, Metzudat David and Meiri cite. 'Over sacrifice' puts the sacrifice at the heart of the oath: this is the ritual, and the next verses will say what it does and does not mean.

The KJV's 'saints' is a theological word with later baggage; these are loyal covenant members, not holy persons. 'By sacrifice' also hides 'over': the sacrifice is the place where the covenant was cut, not the price of it. The aside to hold on to: the gathering is for judgment, and the 'faithful' will find that they are the accused.

philological_notes.note: 'My faithful ones, my loyal ones': those bound to God by chesed, covenant loyalty. KJV 'saints' adds a later technical sense.
Literally 'cutters of my covenant': the standard Hebrew idiom for making a covenant, tied to the cutting of sacrificial animals. Rashi and Meiri tie it to the blood of the covenant at Sinai.
'Over a sacrifice' (YLT). Ibn Ezra reads it as 'because of a sacrifice'; KJV 'by sacrifice' is a looser reading.

verses.translation_literal: And [the] heavens declared his righteousness, for God, judge [is] he. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the heavens take up the word and proclaim his justice, for it is God himself, God and no other, who sits as judge. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The heavens, already called as witnesses in verse 4, now give their testimony. Play it as a hush after the summons: the silent sky is the first to speak, and what it says is a verdict about the judge, not about the accused. In the ancient Near East heavens and earth were the standard witnesses to a treaty, so this is the court's own witness bench.

The last clause is where KJV's 'God is judge himself' is both right and misleading. The Hebrew has the word הוּא, 'he', after 'God ... judge': a resumptive pronoun that puts the whole weight on the speaker, 'God, judge is he'. English 'himself' gives that emphasis. KJV's 'shall declare' also makes it a future; the verb is a waw-consecutive, narrating in the past as if the event had already happened, so the sky has already spoken. Malbim notes that on earth people believe God wants thousands of rams, but in heaven, where there is no eating and drinking, the heavens testify to the justice of this verdict. 'Selah' is a musical or liturgical marker of uncertain meaning, probably a pause or lifting of the voice.

philological_notes.note: A resumptive pronoun after the clause 'God ... judge', giving it emphasis: 'God, judge is he'. KJV 'judge himself' captures it. There is a single pronoun in the verse, not a doubled one.
'And they declared', with the wayyiqtol form that narrates the past. Radak says the open waw here marks a past form standing for a future event, a certain one.
Liturgical marker of uncertain meaning. Malbim reads it as the end of the call and the point where the rebuke now begins.

verses.translation_literal: Hear, my people, and let me speak; Israel, and let me testify against you: God, your God, I [am].
verses.translation_dramatic: Listen, my people, and I will speak. Israel, I will bear witness against you. I am God. I am your God.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the judge turns from the court to the defendants, and the register changes from announcement to direct address. 'Hear, my people' sounds like the opening of the covenant (Deut 6:4, 'Hear, O Israel'), and the accused are those who were promised, 'I will be your God'. The verb 'I will testify' (ve-a'idah) is the verb of a witness giving formal warning with a penalty attached; Meiri ties it to Gen 43:3, 'the man solemnly warned us'. The KJV 'I will testify against thee' is right; ASV's 'unto thee' weakens it.

The last clause is the most important: 'God, your God, I' puts the divine title twice before the pronoun, as a claim of authority first and relationship second. Malbim reads the two halves as matching the two roles: 'I am God' means I cannot be fed by your sacrifices, 'your God' means I am your judge. Play it slowly, with weight on 'your'.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of 'ud, 'to bear witness, give solemn warning'; with the preposition b- it means 'against you'. Metzudat Zion: a warning that is customarily made before witnesses.

verses.translation_literal: Not on your sacrifices do I rebuke you, and your burnt offerings [are] before me continually.
verses.translation_dramatic: It is not your sacrifices I am rebuking you for. Your burnt offerings are not what I count against you; they smoke before me, day after day, and I am not weighing them.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the pivot of the whole psalm. After the thunder of the opening, the judge turns to his own people and the first thing he says is a surprise: this is not a trial about sacrifice. Play the line low and dry, not angry. The hearers expect to be accused of neglect; they are told, in effect, that the ritual is not the issue.

The verse has an awkward second half, and the English versions split over it. The Hebrew just says 'and your burnt offerings before me continually' with no verb. KJV and Webster keep the negative running ('nor ... thy burnt offerings'); YLT and ASV make it a concession ('thy burnt-offerings are continually before me'). Most of the medieval commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David) read the 'not' as still governing 'your burnt offerings': I do not rebuke you for failing to bring them. Malbim alone reads it as concessive, 'indeed your burnt offerings are before me always, since you keep bringing them', and then asks what they are for. The dramatic layer takes the first reading. Either way the point is the same: the burnt offering (עולה, the whole offering that goes up entire) was the daily, constant tāmîd rite, the backbone of Temple worship, and the speaker does not rest his case there.

philological_notes.note: 'I rebuke you', also 'I argue my case against you'. A legal verb: the act of bringing a charge in a dispute. BBE's 'take up a cause against you' brings out the courtroom sense.
'Continually'. It is also the word for the daily burnt offering (the tamid), so the audience would hear a reference to the regular Temple service as well as the adverb.

'And your burnt offerings', with no verb or negative of its own. Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David take the earlier 'not' as still governing it; Malbim takes it as a concessive statement that they are always before God.

verses.translation_literal: I will not take from your house a young bull, from your pens he-goats.
verses.translation_dramatic: I will take no bull out of your house, no he-goats from your pens.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two prize animals of an altar are named, and God refuses to be paid in them: the bull (par) was the costly sacrifice, the male goat the mark of a worthy flock. Radak says each is the biggest of its kind, so the refusal is a refusal of the best. For a farmer, a young bull was capital, and a household gave one only for great occasions; hearing God say he will not take it is to hear him decline a year's wealth.

The KJV 'bullock' is a gentle word for what the Hebrew calls a young adult bull, and 'folds' for the pens is correct. The verb 'take' (laqach) is the verb of seizure and also of accepting a gift: God will neither demand nor accept it as though he needed it. Rashi gives the reason in one line: they are not yours, but mine.

philological_notes.note: 'Your pens' (sheepfolds), from kl' 'to hold back, confine'; cf. Hab 3:17, which Rashi and Meiri cite.
Male goats, the largest of the goats according to Radak and Metzudat Zion.

verses.translation_literal: For to me [belongs] every beast of [the] forest, [the] animals on [the] mountains of a thousand.
verses.translation_dramatic: For every creature of the forest is mine, and the herds that roam the mountains, thousands of them, are mine too.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker widens the lens from the farmyard to the wilderness. In verse 9 he refused bulls and goats from the household; now he says that everything beyond the farmer's fences, the forest and the far hills, already belongs to him. The point is ownership: a worshipper cannot give God something that he already has. Play it with calm, almost amused authority.

Two things are worth noting. First, KJV's 'cattle upon a thousand hills' is a smooth guess; the Hebrew 'mountains of a thousand' is awkward, with the number second. Radak and Meiri read it as 'a thousand mountains', mountains so many that you cannot go among them. Ibn Ezra and Rashi list other readings: a thousand parasangs, or a name, 'a thousand bulls'. The reading Rashi gives anonymously ('some explain') and Ibn Ezra attributes to Rabbi Moshe is the one that takes 'alef' as the 'herds' of Deut 7:13 (שגר אלפיך), 'mountains full of cattle', because the previous verse mentioned the bull. Metzudat David quotes the rabbis that this is the wild ox of Job 40:15 that feeds on a thousand hills a day. Second, 'beast of the forest' has an archaic ending (-ו), which Radak calls an extra waw; it is a fossilized old case ending, not a pronoun.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'on mountains of a thousand'. Readings: 'a thousand mountains' (Radak, Meiri; Metzudat David), 'a thousand parasangs', a name 'a thousand bulls', or 'mountains full of cattle' (Rabbi Moshe cited by Ibn Ezra; Rashi anonymously) by analogy with 'the herds of your cattle' in Deut 7:13.
'Beast of'; the final vav is an old case ending on a construct form, which Ibn Ezra and Radak call an added vav.

verses.translation_literal: I know every bird of [the] mountains, and [the] moving things of [the] field [are] with me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I know every bird in the mountains, every small thing that stirs across the fields. They are all with me.
verses.directors_commentary:
From the herds to the wing and the wriggle. 'I know' is more than awareness: in Hebrew, knowing is care and claim, as God 'knows' Israel in Amos 3:2. Radak says: I know what you do not know. No human catalogue covers every bird of the high crags, and Ibn Ezra adds that these live far from settlement where no one has ever hunted them.

The unusual word is ziz, 'moving thing', which the commentators derive from zuz, 'to move' (Rashi, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion). It is a general term for whatever darts or crawls across a field; the KJV's 'wild beasts' makes it bigger and fiercer than it is. Radak preserves a midrash of a vast bird with its wings spread, but treat that as a later reading. 'Are with me' is gentler than the KJV 'are mine': the Hebrew puts them beside God, in his company and care, not in a ledger.

philological_notes.note: 'Moving things of the field': ziz is derived from zuz 'to move' (Rashi, Metzudat Zion); sadai is a poetic form of sadeh 'field'. KJV 'wild beasts' is an interpretation.
'I know': a perfect that states a standing fact; in Hebrew, knowing includes caring for and claiming, so the verb makes ownership personal.

verses.translation_literal: If I were hungry, I would not say [it] to you, for to me [belongs] [the] world and its fullness.
verses.translation_dramatic: And if I were hungry, would I tell you? The whole world is mine, and everything that fills it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The argument closes with an irony, and the irony is the point. In every culture around Israel, the gods were fed: Mesopotamian temples set out meals for the divine statues twice a day, and the sacrificial system there assumed a hungry god. This psalm says the God of Israel is not that god. Even supposing he were hungry, you would be the last one he would ask, because the whole world is his larder.

The KJV 'If I were hungry, I would not tell thee' is accurate, and the point of the line is its comedy: a god who has to ask the farmer for supper. 'The world and its fullness' (tevel umelo'ah) is a pair of words for the inhabited earth and all that fills it. Ibn Ezra puts it as an argument from lesser to greater: even a man in need would not ask from someone who has little, so how much less does God, who has everything. Play it dry, almost amused, then let the weight fall on 'mine'.

philological_notes.note: 'The world and its fullness': tevel is the inhabited world, melo'ah is from ml' 'to fill'. Metzudat David reads 'fullness' as the creatures that fill the world.

verses.translation_literal: Shall I eat the flesh of mighty ones, and the blood of he-goats shall I drink?
verses.translation_dramatic: Do you think I am hungry? Do you picture me bent over the flesh of your great bulls, tipping back my head to drink the blood of your he-goats?
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker is the God of Israel, and the question is not a request for information but a rebuke, dropped into the room like a stone. In the ancient Near East the idea that gods eat was the ordinary one: Mesopotamian and Canaanite temples set out meals for their gods every day, and the sacrificial system of the neighbours rested on the notion that the gods needed feeding. Here YHWH laughs at the idea. Say the line with real incredulity, with a half-smile.

The KJV's 'bulls' and 'goats' are fair, but 'will I eat' reads like a mild doubt. The Hebrew has two questions, one for the flesh and one for the blood, and the blood is the sharper image, because blood is the life that the Torah reserves for God and forbids to the people. To have God drink it is to make him a monster. Note the rhythm: eat... drink, a matched pair, each with its victim. The word אַבִּירִים ('mighty ones') is used of fighting men, horses and bulls alike, so the beasts brought to the altar are called by their strength: the best, the prize, and for all that useless to the one who is offered them.

philological_notes.note: 'Mighty, strong ones', used of bulls here as the strong of the herd; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri read it as 'bulls', Metzudat Zion glosses it 'strong'. The same root gives 'the Mighty One of Jacob'.
Adult he-goats, the leaders of the flock.

verses.translation_literal: Sacrifice to God a thank-offering, and pay to the Most High your vows.
verses.translation_dramatic: No. Bring me thanks: let that be the sacrifice you lay before God. And what you have vowed, pay it in full to the Most High.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the mocking questions comes the positive command, and the pace slows. The Hebrew sets two imperatives side by side, 'sacrifice' and 'pay', each with its own divine title, God and the Most High. The thank-offering (תּוֹדָה) is a sacrifice of the shared-meal type, eaten by the worshipper with family and friends, and it goes with a public confession of what God has done; the word means both 'thanks' and 'confession'. It is the offering of someone who has been rescued. It is not a payment to feed a god.

The KJV 'Offer unto God thanksgiving' softens a verb that is specifically 'slaughter, sacrifice' (זָבַח); the Hebrew has no 'offer'. And 'pay' (שַׁלֵּם) is the commercial verb for settling a debt, the same root as 'peace' and 'whole': a vow is a loan taken from God in a moment of need, and now the bill comes. Rashi and Radak, and Metzudat David, read the thank-offering as a confession of sins, which is one reading of 'confession'; the plain sense is gratitude.

philological_notes.note: Thanks, praise and confession in one word, and the name of a sacrifice eaten as a meal. The sense 'confession of sin' is found in Rashi, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David on this verse; the plain sense here is the thank-offering of the one who has been saved.
'Pay in full, make whole'; the verb for settling a vow or debt, from the root of shalom.

verses.translation_literal: And call me in a day of trouble; I will rescue you, and you will honor me.
verses.translation_dramatic: And when the day of trouble comes, call to me. I will pull you out of it, and you will give me honor.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the heart of the covenant bargain as the psalm sees it, and it is spoken without threat: call, and I will rescue. Three verbs in a chain, the first an imperative, the next two futures, make a promise that is also an exchange, because the rescued man is to honor the one who rescued him, which is what the thank-offering of verse 14 is for. The 'day of trouble' (יוֹם צָרָה) is a narrow place, from a root meaning to be tight, and the picture is of someone stuck in a pass.

The KJV 'deliver' and 'glorify' are accurate but a little ecclesiastical. חָלַץ means to pull out, to draw out of danger, as one draws off a sandal or draws a soldier out of the line; כִּבֵּד has the root of 'weight' (כָּבֵד), so to 'honor' is to give someone weight, to treat him as heavy in the community. In a shame-and-honor society this is the whole point: God gets his reputation, and the man gets his life. Rashi hears it as God's honor being that he saves those who trust him.

philological_notes.note: 'I will draw you out, rescue'; the piel, with the sense of pulling someone out of a tight place. The same verb is used for drawing off a sandal and for the armed men who go out ahead.
'You will honor me', literally 'give me weight'; from the root of 'heavy' and 'glory'. Rashi reads God's honor as his saving those who trust him.

verses.translation_literal: And to the wicked God said, What is to you to recount my decrees, and you have taken my covenant on your mouth?
verses.translation_dramatic: But then God turns to the wicked. 'What right have you to recite my statutes? What business have you with my covenant on your lips?'
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm turns here, with a heavy beat: up to now God has spoken to the faithful who bring their offerings, and now the second audience, the wicked, is addressed. The Hebrew begins with 'and to the wicked' (וְלָרָשָׁע) set before the verb, so the person is put forward, as if the speaker has swung round to face him. The question מַה־לְּךָ, literally 'what to you?', is an idiom for 'what right, what business have you?' and has the tone of a bouncer at a door.

The man is not an outsider; he recites the law and carries the covenant in his mouth. The Hebrew says 'lift' (וַתִּשָּׂא) your mouth-covenant, the verb used for 'lift up the name' in the Third Commandment: to pronounce it, to wield it. The KJV's 'take my covenant in thy mouth' is a little limp, and its 'or that thou shouldest' turns the second clause into a hypothetical, whereas Hebrew says 'and you take': it is the fact of the man's behavior that is questioned, in a charge. Radak and Metzudat David read the failing as speech without heart; Meiri catches it in 'on your mouth' and not in your heart. Malbim reads the 'statutes' as the ritual commands, which the wicked man performs in place of the ethical ones.

philological_notes.note: Idiom, 'what is it to you?', meaning 'what right or business have you'.
'On your mouth': the covenant rests on the lips and goes no deeper. Meiri draws the point that it is 'on your mouth' and not in your heart.

verses.translation_literal: And you, you hated discipline, and you threw my words behind you.
verses.translation_dramatic: And you? You hate to be corrected. My words you flung over your shoulder and walked on.
verses.directors_commentary:
'And you' (וְאַתָּה) is the accusing finger, a pronoun placed at the front for emphasis. The charge has two verbs, hate and throw, and a clear picture: the man hears the instruction and tosses it behind him, where he need not look at it. In a culture where the road ahead is the place of what one sees and the back is the place of what one ignores, to throw something 'behind you' is to put it out of sight and out of mind. A related idiom, 'behind the back', appears in Nehemiah 9:26 for the prophets whose Torah the people threw away.

מוּסָר, which the KJV renders 'instruction', is more than information: it is discipline, correction, the training that comes with a rod. This is something the hearer does not just forget, but dislikes. The KJV's 'Seeing thou hatest' turns the accusation into a clause of reason, 'since', where the Hebrew states it flat: you hate. Note the tense: a perfect, 'you hated', a settled stance. Radak and Malbim split the terms: 'discipline' for duties to fellow men, 'words' for the rest.

philological_notes.note: Discipline, correction, training by chastening; more than the KJV's 'instruction'. Radak reads it as the commandments between man and his fellow; Meiri as the Torah whose ways are ways of pleasantness and discipline.
'You threw my words behind you': to put out of sight and out of mind. Metzudat David: as a man throws away what he does not want to see.

verses.translation_literal: If you saw a thief, then you were pleased with him, and with adulterers [was] your portion.
verses.translation_dramatic: You saw a thief, and you were glad of his company. You cast your lot in with adulterers.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the charge becomes specific, and it cites two of the Ten Commandments, theft and adultery. The man does not necessarily steal himself; he sees a thief and is pleased with him, takes pleasure in him, goes along. 'Portion' (חֵלֶק) is the word for a share of land or a share of loot: the accused has put his inheritance among the adulterers, as in the lot of the tribe. The psalm's God holds not only the doer but the one who approves.

The KJV, ASV and Webster's 'thou consentedst' and 'partaker' are fair, but 'consentedst' is a heavy archaism and the Hebrew is a plain 'were pleased'. Note the word-play inside וַתִּרֶץ: the verb can be heard as רצה 'be pleased' (Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat Zion) or as רוץ 'run', and the Targum, which has 'you ran after him', takes the second. Ibn Ezra allows both. The ambiguity is useful for an actor: pleasure and pursuit, the glad eye and the quick step.

philological_notes.note: Most read 'you were pleased, consented' (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion); Ibn Ezra and Meiri also record a reading from רוץ 'run', which the Targum follows ('you ran after him').
'Your portion, your share': the word for a share of the land, spoil or inheritance. Metzudat David: you chose your portion in walking with adulterers.

verses.translation_literal: Your mouth you sent out in evil, and your tongue it yokes deceit.
verses.translation_dramatic: Your mouth you loose on evil, and your tongue is harnessed to lies.
verses.directors_commentary: From the hands to the mouth: the accused is now convicted of speech. Mouth first, pushed to the front of the line, then tongue, and a pair of strong verbs, 'send out' and 'yoke'. The Hebrew says 'you sent your mouth into evil', as one lets a dog off the leash or sends an animal into a field; the KJV's 'givest thy mouth to evil' is blander. Then 'tongue ... yokes deceit' (תַּצְמִיד מִרְמָה): צָמַד is to bind two things together under one yoke, from the noun for a pair of oxen or a bracelet or a lid fastened tight (Numbers 19:15, 'a covering fastened' in Rashi's note). The tongue, then, pulls deceit alongside itself like a team; a lie and a tongue ploughing the same furrow. The KJV's 'frameth' loses all of this. The mouth is also the thing which carried God's covenant in verse 16, so the man's one organ serves two masters.

philological_notes.note: 'Yoke, join, bind together' (a pair); Rashi, Metzudat Zion and Radak all connect it to 'joining', and Rashi to צָמִיד פָּתִיל of Numbers 19:15, a sealed covering. Meiri: the lies are joined and ready in the mouth.
'You sent out, let loose': the mouth is sent like a messenger or let go like an animal. Radak: as if freed from the restraint of speaking evil.

verses.translation_literal: You sit; against your brother you speak; against the son of your mother you give a fault.
verses.translation_dramatic: You sit, at your ease, and you talk. Against your brother, you talk. Against the son of your own mother, you hand out blame.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two verbs of sitting and speaking are set down bare, with no 'and' between them, so the picture is of someone settled in a seat, unhurried, talking. Rashi takes the sitting as a seat among scoffers (Rashi on Psalm 50:20), and Ibn Ezra reads it the same way, adding that the speaker has sent his harm to people who are not even his kin. Directors should play this as habit rather than outburst: the accuser has a regular place to sit and a regular audience.

The KJV joins the two halves with 'and' and renders the second as 'slanderest', which is a fair sense but loses the line's two-step shape. The Hebrew says 'you give a fault' (titen dofi): the speaker hands out a blemish to someone, as one hands over goods. Dofi is a rare word for a stain or a charge of disgrace; Rashi ties it to the verb for thrusting away, meaning something shameful said in order to push the person off (Rashi on Psalm 50:20, with Numbers 35:20). The KJV's 'thine own mother's son' adds the word 'own', which the Hebrew does not have, though the sense of closeness is right.

The pairing 'brother' and 'son of your mother' is a step inward, not a repeat. Rashi reads the second as a particular kind of brother, one with whom you have no case or quarrel because he does not inherit alongside you. Radak reads the line as covering the son of your father and the son of your mother alike, even though no dealings lie between you, since your inheritance is not shared. Metzudat David reads it as a rising scale of closeness: you speak ill even of your brother, even of the son of your mother, who is surely your brother. For the actor the point is the same on all three readings: the circle of people spared by this speaker's tongue is zero.

philological_notes.note: A rare noun for a blemish or stain, used here for a charge of disgrace. Rashi connects it with the root of 'thrust away', so a shameful thing said to push someone aside. Radak calls it an expression of reviling and abuse, and Metzudat Zion glosses it as words of disgrace. The verb 'give' makes the charge something handed to the victim.
'Against the son of your mother', set parallel to 'against your brother'. The commentators differ on what kind of brother it names; see the commentary for the three readings.

verses.translation_literal: These you have done, and I kept silent; you imagined, being, I will be like you; I will rebuke you, and I will arrange [it] before your eyes.
verses.translation_dramatic: All this you did, and I said nothing. And you thought, 'He is the same as I am.' But now I will confront you. I will lay it all out in rows before your eyes.
verses.directors_commentary:
The most daring verse of the psalm, and the turning point of the whole speech. God's silence is not consent: 'I kept silent' (הֶחֱרַשְׁתִּי) is the silence of patience, and the man has mistaken patience for approval. The sentence that follows, 'you imagined that I would be like you', is the great charge: you reasoned that the one who does not punish must be as lax, as tolerant of evil, as you. Many commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri) hear in this 'you thought I do not see the hidden things as you do not'. Moral pride becomes a theological error: remaking God in your own image.

The Hebrew doubles the verb, הֱיוֹת אֶהְיֶה, 'being, I will be', an emphatic form: you thought I surely would be like you. The KJV's 'altogether such an one as thyself' captures the force. Then the court scene: 'I will rebuke you' (אוֹכִיחֲךָ) is the lawsuit verb, and 'I will arrange' (אֶעֶרְכָה) is to set in order, to line up, as soldiers are drawn up or as a case is set out in order. The KJV supplies 'them' after 'set in order', which is fair, since Hebrew leaves the object out and the sins are meant. Meiri: as if it were written down in front of him. Play the line with a slow, almost gentle menace; no shouting.

philological_notes.note: 'I kept silent': the silence of forbearance. Ibn Ezra: because I am long-suffering it is as if I were silent; Metzudat David: from punishing you.
'I will set in order, arrange, lay out': used of drawing up a battle line and of setting out a legal case; Metzudat Zion: 'arranging'. Meiri: as if written before him.

verses.translation_literal: Consider this, please, [you] forgetters of Eloah, lest I tear, and there is none to deliver.
verses.translation_dramatic: Think on this, I beg you, you who forget God, before I tear you apart and there is no one left to pull you free.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the accusation, the warning, and with it a softening: 'please' (נָא) is the courteous particle of a request, which sits strangely beside the threat that follows, and shows the speaker still wishes for a hearing. The audience is now the whole class of the guilty, 'those who forget Eloah': not atheists, but people who live as if God were not there, like those who forget a debt. Eloah is a rare singular for God, found mostly in Job and the poetic books.

The verb אֶטְרֹף is the word for what a lion or wolf does with prey: to tear in pieces. The KJV's 'lest I tear you in pieces' is right, and the 'you' is not in the Hebrew. Ibn Ezra draws on the shepherd who can save a lamb from a bear or wolf, but not from the lion. 'None to deliver' (אֵין מַצִּיל) is a legal-military phrase, with an echo of verse 15's 'I will rescue': the only one who could rescue is the one who is tearing. Deliver the line low and quiet, as a last warning.

philological_notes.note: Singular form of the divine title, rarer than אֱלֹהִים and found mostly in poetry and Job.
'I will tear to pieces', as a beast of prey. Ibn Ezra takes it as the lion's tearing, from which the shepherd cannot save.

verses.translation_literal: One who sacrifices a thank-offering honors me, and one who sets a way, I will let him look on the salvation of God.
verses.translation_dramatic: Whoever brings the thank-offering, and brings it with thanks, gives me honor. And the one who sets his way straight before him — to that one I will show the salvation of God.
verses.directors_commentary:
After twenty-two verses of charge and warning, this is the first open door, and it is the last line of the psalm. Play it as a change of temperature: the voice that threatened to tear in the verse before now offers. The structure is two halves in balance. One who sacrifices a thank-offering honors me; one who sets a way, I will make him see salvation. The first half names the offering the psalm has been testing (vv. 8–15): the תּוֹדָה, a communal meal of thanksgiving, eaten by the offerer and his guests on the day it was offered (Lev 7:12–15). It was not a payment to feed God, a point the psalm has already made with scorn. What honors him is the thanks.

The second half is harder, and the commentators split. 'Sets a way' is bare in the Hebrew: דֶּרֶךְ has no adjective. The KJV 'ordereth his conversation aright' adds 'aright' and uses 'conversation' in its old sense of 'conduct'; the Hebrew says only 'sets a way'. Rashi takes it as one who returns, to whom God teaches 'and sets a way' for sinners to come back. Radak reads the man himself as the subject: one who sets his way and heart straight, so that he needs no sacrifice at all. Metzudat David reads it as one who does not act by chance but fixes eyes and heart on his road, to weigh whether it is good or bad. Radak also records a midrash that reads the word with a shin, 'one who weighs his ways', from שׁוּמָא, 'estimate'; the Masoretic text points it with sin, 'sets'. Both readings lead to the same conduct.

The last words, 'the salvation of God', have God speaking of himself in the third person, 'I will let him look... on the salvation of God', where one expects 'my salvation'. Radak and Metzudat David both treat this as a normal biblical manner, compared with 'and to Moses he said, Come up to the LORD' (Exod 24:1). Do not play it as distance; the voice stays his own.

philological_notes.note: 'And one who sets a way.' The MT points the participle with sin, from שׂוּם 'to set, place'. Radak records a midrash that reads it with shin, from שׁוּמָא 'estimation': one who weighs his ways so that they are upright and just toward people. The Masoretic reading is followed here. Ibn Ezra compares 'they set their hearts and gave heed' and takes it as 'to whom the straight way has become clear'.

'Thanksgiving, a thank-offering.' The same word means both the thanks spoken and the sacrifice that carries them. Radak and Rashi read it as the offering that comes with an admission of wrongdoing. Metzudat David reads it as an offering brought with confession and a return from sin. The verse does not pick between thanks and confession.

'In the salvation of God.' After 'I will let him look' God names himself in the third person. Ibn Ezra explains it as 'in my salvation'; Metzudat David calls it the usual manner of Scripture and compares Exod 24:1. Radak adds that the time of salvation is the day of judgment.
